content: The ACADS gene encodes the enzyme acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, C-2 to C-3 short chain, which is a tetrameric mitochondrial flavoprotein. This enzyme belongs to the acyl-CoA dehydrogenase family and is responsible for catalyzing the initial step of mitochondrial fatty acid beta-oxidation. Mutations in the ACADS gene are associated with short-chain acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency (SCADD). The ACADS gene spans approximately 13 kilobases (kb) and contains 10 exons. Its coding sequence is 1239 base pairs (bp) in length. The SCAD enzyme specifically acts on short-chain fatty acids, particularly those between C2 and C3 acyl-CoA, by forming a C2-C3 trans-double bond through dehydrogenation. The end product of beta-oxidation is acetyl-CoA. When the SCAD enzyme is misfolded due to defects, there is an increase in reactive oxygen species (ROS) production. This elevated ROS level induces mitochondrial fission, leading to a grain-like structure in the mitochondrial reticulum. Mutations in the ACADS gene result in SCAD deficiency, also known as butyryl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency. Numerous mutations have been identified in specific populations, and large-scale studies have been conducted to determine the allelic and genotypic frequencies of the defective gene. SCAD deficiency, as it impairs beta-oxidation, leads to an accumulation of fatty acids. This condition is characterized by elevated levels of butyrylcarnitine (C4) in blood plasma and increased ethylmalonic acid (EMA) concentrations in urine. The genotypes of affected individuals may result from a mutation, a variant, or a combination of both. In one population with SCAD deficiency, three subgroups have been identified. The first group exhibits failure to thrive, feeding difficulties, and hypotonia. The second group experiences seizures, while the third group has hypotonia without seizures. Other studies have shown that SCAD deficiency may be asymptomatic under normal conditions, with symptoms manifesting only under physiological stress, such as fasting or illness. Treatment for SCAD deficiency can be challenging due to its sometimes asymptomatic nature. Management typically involves restoring biochemical and physiological homeostasis, promoting anabolism, and providing alternative energy sources, similar to treatments for other fatty acid oxidation disorders. Flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) supplementation has been identified as a potential therapy, as FAD is an essential cofactor for proper SCAD function. SCAD deficiency is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Carrier testing can be performed for at-risk family members, and prenatal testing is also an option. The ACADS gene has also been implicated in delaying the onset of Prader-Willi Syndrome, a condition characterized by hypotonia, growth failure, and neurodevelopmental delays in early life, followed by hyperphagia and obesity later in life. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have linked SCAD with reduced insulin release, as demonstrated by oral glucose tolerance tests (OGTT).
